title: Perceptrons and backpropagation
subtitle: One neuron draws a line. Stack layers and the network can draw any boundary — if you can train it.

sections.title: The artificial neuron
sections.body: A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, z = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b, then applies an activation function: step (perceptron), sigmoid 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), tanh, or ReLU max(0, z). Without a non-linearity, any stack of layers collapses into one linear map.

questions.prompt: Why do we need a non-linear activation?

choices.text: Stacked linear layers are equivalent to a single linear layer.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Non-linearity is what gives depth its power.

sections.title: What one neuron can and cannot do
sections.body: A perceptron’s decision boundary is a straight line (hyperplane). It learns AND (converged: yes) but cannot learn XOR — Minsky and Papert’s 1969 observation which stalled the field. The cure is a hidden layer.

questions.prompt: Why can a single perceptron not compute XOR?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Two inputs are enough for AND.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A hidden layer combines two lines.

sections.title: Multilayer networks and backpropagation
sections.body: A multilayer perceptron has hidden layers between input and output. Backpropagation trains it: (1) forward pass computes the output; (2) the loss measures the error; (3) the chain rule sends the error gradient backwards, layer by layer, giving ∂L/∂w for every weight; (4) gradient descent updates w ← w − η ∂L/∂w. Run the 2-3-1 network on XOR: the loss falls to 0.0004 and all four outputs are right (yes).

worked.why: Output unit: y = σ(z), loss E = ½(y − t)². Its error signal is δ = (y − t)·y(1 − y).
For a hidden unit h the signal is passed back through the weight: δ_h = δ_o · w · h(1 − h).
Each weight moves against its gradient: Δw = −η δ · (input to that weight).

choices.text: The gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, using the chain rule backwards.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The update then follows by gradient descent.

figures.caption: Figure 5.3.1 — learning XOR
figures.note: Line thickness is |weight|; watch the loss curve fall.

problems.prompt: After training, do all four XOR inputs give outputs on the correct side of 0.5?
problems.answer: Yes: the trained network reports solved = yes with loss 0.0004.

sections.title: Deep learning and architectures
sections.body: Deep learning uses many layers that learn features automatically. Convolutional networks share small filters across an image (translation-invariant features); recurrent networks carry a hidden state through a sequence; transformers replace recurrence with attention. Universal approximation: one hidden layer of enough units can approximate any continuous function — depth makes it efficient. Generative networks (GANs, diffusion models, language models) create new data.

questions.prompt: Why do convolutional layers suit images?

choices.text: They reuse the same small filter everywhere, detecting a feature wherever it appears.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — a CNN pipeline
figures.note: A convolutional classifier in four stages.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Neuron = weighted sum + activation; a single neuron separates linearly only.
  • Hidden layers + backpropagation solve XOR and far more.

sections.title: Try it
sections.body: In the card below set units to 2 and then 1 and see what happens to the loss: how many hidden units does XOR need?

questions.prompt: A network with ONE hidden unit and a sigmoid output on XOR…

choices.text: Cannot reach zero error: a single hidden unit gives only one new feature.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: XOR needs at least two hidden units.

figures.caption: Figure 5.6.1 — two hidden units
figures.note: Two hidden units can solve XOR — but some random starts get stuck in a local minimum (try seed 3).
